explanation.dictionary: The informal positive nonpast is the dictionary form itself.
explanation.past-plain: The informal past is the te-form with the last vowel changed to an a-sound (て → た, で → だ).
explanation.conditional-negative: Negative conditional: negative form with ない → なければ.

te-form.1: The te-form of a godan verb depends on the last syllable: う・つ・る → って, く → いて, ぐ → いで, ぶ・む・ぬ → んで, す → して.
te-form.2: Te-form: replace る with て.
te-form.3: Irregular: する → して, くる → きて.
te-form.i-adjective: Te-form: replace い with くて.

tai-form.all: Tai-form: masu-stem + たい, which then conjugates like an i-adjective.

tari-form.i-adjective: Tari-form: replace い with かったり.

volitional.1: Volitional: change the final u-sound to the o-row and add う (う → おう).
volitional.2: Volitional: replace る with よう.
volitional.3: Irregular: する → しよう, くる → こよう.

potential.1: Potential: change the final u-sound to the e-row and add る (う → える).
potential.2: Potential: replace る with られる.
potential.3: Irregular: する → できる, くる → こられる.

imperative.1: Imperative: change the final u-sound to the e-row (う → え).
imperative.2: Imperative: replace る with ろ.
imperative.3: Irregular: する → しろ, くる → こい.

conditional.all: Conditional: change the final u-sound to the e-row and add ば (…れば).
conditional.i-adjective: Conditional: replace い with ければ.

passive.2: Passive: replace る with られる.
passive.3: Irregular: する → される, くる → こられる.

causative.2: Causative: replace る with させる.
causative.3: Irregular: する → させる, くる → こさせる.

caus-pass.1: Causative-passive: negative stem + せられる.
caus-pass.2: Causative-passive: replace る with させられる.
caus-pass.3: Irregular: する → させられる, くる → こさせられる.

explanation.polite-endings: Formal endings: ます, ません (negative), ました (past), ませんでした (negative past).
explanation.nai-endings: Negative: stem + ない; negative past: なかった.
explanation.i-adjective-normal: I-adjective endings: い → くない (negative), かった (past), くなかった (negative past); formal adds です.
explanation.na-adjective-normal: Na-adjective: the copula is conjugated: だ, ではない, だった, ではなかった; formal です, ではありません, でした, ではありませんでした.

title.home: Katsu: practise Japanese conjugation and kanji - 活用
title.kanji-practice: All kanji with stroke order - Katsu

information.title: How Katsu works
information.lead: Katsu (活用, katsuyō: conjugation) is two free trainers in one app: an endless stream of conjugation questions, and kanji writing practice in the correct stroke order. Free, no account, works offline.

how.title: Conjugation in three steps
how.step1: Choose what to practise: forms, word types and your JLPT level. You can change them at any time, even mid-session.
how.step2: Type your answer in the 答え field. Romaji is converted to hiragana as you type, so a Japanese keyboard is not needed. Hiragana, katakana and kanji are all accepted.
how.step3: Press enter to check. Correct answers turn green; mistakes show the right answer with a step-by-step explanation. Press enter again for the next question.

kanji.title: Writing kanji in three steps
kanji.step1: Every kanji starts with a lesson: watch the stroke order, trace the character once, then write it from memory.
kanji.step2: Draw on the pad with your finger or mouse. Each stroke is checked for shape, order and direction, and hints are there when you are stuck.
kanji.step3: Learned kanji come back as reviews, spaced from four hours out to four months. Written cleanly, they stay away longer; Your devices carries the schedule to another device.

description.home: Katsu is a free practice app for Japanese: drill verb and adjective conjugation from JLPT N5 to N1, and learn to write kanji in the correct stroke order.
description.information: How Katsu works: an endless stream of Japanese conjugation questions and kanji writing practice with stroke order, explained in three steps each.
description.about: Katsu is made by Arthur Hoek, a Dutch developer. The app is free and open source (MIT). Contact, GitHub and tip links.
description.kanji: Practise writing the 1026 kanji Japanese children learn in their six years of primary school, stroke by stroke, in the correct stroke order.
description.kanji-practice: Every one of the 1026 kanji Japanese children learn in their six years of primary school, each with its stroke order written out and a pad to write it on yourself.

about.title: About the maker
about.lead: Hi! I'm Arthur Hoek, a developer from the Netherlands. I built Katsu to make drilling Japanese conjugation less of a chore (and because I needed it myself).
